records.name: Punjab
records.current_summary: Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade at the Rose Garden after "mounting resistance" from Sikh religious organisations, specifically the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht — the faith's highest temporal authority. Organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason for cancelling the annual event. Amritsar is the spiritual centre of Sikhism, and the Akal Takht exercises quasi-governmental power over public assembly within its sphere, making this a state-implicated suppression of trans public expression rather than a private dispute.  Against the national 0.43, Punjab sits −0.08. While the single-incident rule counsels caution, this event meets the exception: it is state-implicated (a named authority with effective governmental power compelled the cancellation), it was met with impunity (the event simply did not happen), and it directly suppresses the public visibility a visitor relies on for safety. Compared to Delhi (0.38), which also faces police profiling but maintains India's most visible trans civic presence, Punjab's suppression targets the civic presence itself. Compared to Tamil Nadu (0.53), where a court actively commended trans-affirming policy, Punjab demonstrates the inverse dynamic — religious authority vetoing trans assembly.  No Punjab-specific welfare board or trans-related statute deviation was identified beyond this event (Punjab is absent from the official 12-board list). The finding is narrow but material: a trans visitor attending a public gathering in Amritsar encounters a documented precedent of institutional suppression.

records.name: Kerala
records.current_summary: Kerala was the first state in India to adopt a dedicated Policy for Transgenders, with named welfare measures including an overseas scholarship scheme administered through the Social Justice Department. A constituted welfare board exists. Kerala is one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (2 of 7) and logged 4 of the 11 national cases in 2023, indicating the legal machinery is at least operational and that trans-targeted incidents are being formally registered rather than ignored.  Against the national 0.43, Kerala sits +0.07. The policy infrastructure and scholarship scheme represent genuine state commitment to trans inclusion beyond the federal floor. Compared to Tamil Nadu (0.53), Kerala lacks the additional layer of active judicial endorsement (the Madras High Court commendation) and the longer institutional history since 1995, but its first-state policy status and operational board mark it clearly above the national norm. Compared to Assam (0.45), Kerala's protective framework is more developed and better documented.  For a visitor, the practical benefit is institutional visibility: a trans-presenting person in Kochi or urban Kerala encounters a governance structure that has codified recognition, though like most Indian states, city-level norms in Thiruvananthapuram or Kochi are far more protective than rural areas.

sources.claim: queerbeat data report (30 Jan 2026): per the NCRB, the Transgender Persons Act recorded only 20 cases nationwide 2019-2023 - 1 in Tamil Nadu (2020); 7 in 2021 (2 each in Assam and Kerala, 3 in West Bengal); 1 in Tamil Nadu (2022); 11 in 2023 (7 Tamil Nadu, 4 Kerala), none from north and central India; it attributes the scarcity to police registration bias, against survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence (2025 Transgender Health study, n=4,964).

Press Information Bureau reply in the Rajya Sabha (8 Dec 2021, Minister Dr. Virendra Kumar): 12 states/UTs have constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under section 10(1) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules, 2020 - Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Chandigarh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.

records.name: Assam
records.current_summary: Assam recorded 2 of the 7 national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021, indicating some functioning legal infrastructure for trans-related complaints. The state is part of the Northeast border belt where the infiltration/Bangladeshi-detention script operates — the Panisagar raids ran along the Assam–Agartala highway — though no Assam-specific checkpoint case was identified in this research pass. Assam has NOT constituted a transgender welfare board: per the official 12-board list (Dec 2021) it is among the states/UTs still lacking one.  Against the national 0.43, Assam sits marginally +0.02. The positive signal is thin: recorded cases could indicate either crimes happening or a legal system engaging with them, and the dossier frames the latter reading. The negative ambient signal (proximity to the Tripura/West Bengal border-profiling zone) is not offset by any Assam-specific protective policy comparable to Tamil Nadu or Kerala, and the missing welfare board marks lower official visibility than in the southern states. Compared to West Bengal (0.34), Assam shares the border-belt exposure but lacks the documented trans-as-infiltration arrests; compared to Tripura (0.31), the absence of any named checkpoint operation in Assam is the key differentiator. The deviation is small and confidence is low.

records.name: Ceara
records.current_summary: Ceará is the most consistent lethal hotspot for trans and travesti people in the Northeast: 11 killings in 2024 (3rd nationally, 1st in the region) and 8 in 2025 (tied for the highest state total in the country). Against a population of ~9 million this yields roughly 0.9 killings per million per year—more than double the national rate of ~0.38/million (80 / 213 M). The 2025 dossier further notes a concentration of Black victims in Ceará.  This places Ceará about 0.10 below the national 0.71. The deviation is driven by sustained, patterned lethal exposure rather than any legal distinction (the federal constitution and penal code apply uniformly). Compared with Minas Gerais (0.64), which matched Ceará's absolute 2025 count of 8, Minas Gerais' much larger population (~21 M) gives a per-capita rate at the national average, making Ceará the higher-risk state on a rate basis.  For a visibly trans visitor, the pattern matters: the killings are concentrated on young Black trans women in public space—precisely the exposure profile of a conspicuous traveller—and the consistency across two years signals an entrenched environment rather than a statistical blip.

records.name: Paraiba
records.current_summary: Paraíba recorded 4 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same absolute count as Rio Grande do Norte. Against a population of ~4 million this yields approximately 1.0 per million per year—well above the national rate of ~0.38/million and among the highest in the federation. The state is part of the Northeast bloc that absorbed 38 of 80 national killings (47.5%) in 2025.  The per-capita rate places Paraíba roughly 0.09 below the national 0.71. Compared with Alagoas (0.68), which had 2 killings in a similar population (~3.3 M, rate ~0.61/million), Paraíba's absolute count is double and its rate higher, reflecting the broader Northeast concentration on a smaller denominator.  No Paraíba-specific legal or ordinance evidence was found; the deviation is driven entirely by the violence dataset. The victim profile—young, Black, poor, Northeastern—concentrates risk on individuals who present visibly in public space.

records.name: Pernambuco
records.current_summary: Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, placing it in the second tier behind Ceará/Minas Gerais. Against a population of ~9.4 million this yields roughly 0.74 per million per year—nearly double the national rate. Crucially, the state hosts the major tourist corridor of Recife and Olinda, so the violence concentration directly overlaps with visitor traffic and visible trans presence in public coastal spaces.  The rate and tourism overlap put Pernambuco about 0.07 below the national 0.71. Compared with Bahia (0.65), which also recorded 7 killings in 2025, Bahia's larger population (~15 M) gives a lower per-capita rate of ~0.47/million; Pernambuco's risk density is therefore somewhat higher despite the identical absolute count, and both states share the visitor-coast exposure.  No Pernambuco-specific legal restriction or ordinance was found. The deviation is violence-driven and location-dependent: a trans visitor staying in Recife's centre or the Olinda historic district is in the same geography where the killings cluster.

records.name: Bahia

records.name: Maranhao
records.current_summary: Maranhão recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same count as Goiás and Pará; it also recorded 5 in 2024, so the toll is persistent rather than a one-year spike. Against a population of ~7.1 million the 2025 rate is about 0.70 per million per year, roughly double the national average. Maranhão is one of the poorest states in the federation, and the dossier's victim profile - young, Black, poor and Northeastern - maps directly onto its demographics, indicating the killings track structural exposure rather than incidental misfortune.  No unit-specific ordinance or legal finding was identified; the profile rests on the sustained killing counts. Ceará, the other Northeast state at the top of the 2025 list, recorded 8 killings the same year.

records.name: Para
